summary: For ages 10–11: round decimals to any place and whole numbers to a required degree of accuracy by treating rounding as a nearness decision on a number line. Learners locate the number between its two candidate rounding points, find the midpoint, and decide which it is nearer — deriving the 'look at the next digit' rule from the midpoint rather than memorising it. Work covers decimals to a stated number of places, large whole numbers to a stated place, carry/round-up cascades over a 9, placeholder zeros, the risk of double rounding, and rounding for estimation.
misconceptions: Rounding digit-by-digit / double rounding (3.4567 → 3.457 → 3.46 → 3.5) instead of one decision at the target place
'Always round 5 down' or inconsistent treatment of the exact-midpoint case
Truncating (chopping) rather than rounding (3.48 → 3.4 to 1 dp)
Forgetting the round-up cascade across a 9 (3.798 to 2 dp → 3.80, not 3.79 or 3.710)
Dropping the trailing zero that records the rounded place (writing 3.8 for 3.80 to 2 dp when the place must be shown)

activities.title: Rounding as a nearness decision on a number line
steps: Pick a target precision (e.g. 1 decimal place) and draw a number line showing the two candidate values the number sits between — for 3.4567 to 1 dp, that is 3.4 and 3.5.
Mark the midpoint of the segment (3.45) clearly.
Place the number on the line (3.4567 lands just past the midpoint) and state which candidate it is nearer to.
State the rounded result (3.5) and point to the digit that decided it (the hundredths digit, 5, sits at/past halfway).
Repeat in whole-number mode: bracket 7,654,321 between 7,600,000 and 7,700,000, mark the midpoint 7,650,000, place the number, and round to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000).
Try a round-up cascade: place 3.798 to round to 2 dp between 3.79 and 3.80, see it is nearer 3.80, and write the trailing zero.

Compare two routes for rounding 3.4547 to 2 dp: round straight to 2 dp (decider is the thousandths 4, so 3.45) and also round to 3 dp first (3.455) then to 2 dp (3.46). Notice the answers differ — so make one decision at the target place, not a chain of roundings.
activities.insight: The midpoint IS the '5-and-above' rule: a number at or past halfway rounds up to the higher candidate. Rounding is one decision made at the target place by comparing nearness, not a digit-by-digit chop — and chopping or double rounding can give a different, wrong answer.

activities.title: Isolating the deciding digit with a place-value chart
steps: Write the number in a place-value chart spanning the decimal point.
Circle the place you must round to and underline the single digit immediately beyond it — the decider.
Round 3.4567 to 2 dp (3.46) and say which digit decided it (the 6 in the thousandths).
Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000) and name the deciding digit (the ten-thousands digit, 5).
Count the digits after the point aloud to confirm you gave the asked-for precision (e.g. 2 dp means exactly two decimal digits).
activities.insight: Only the digit one place beyond the required accuracy decides the rounding; naming the target place prevents rounding to the wrong precision.

activities.title: Keeping placeholder zeros after a carry
steps: Round 2.397 to 2 dp. The hundredths carry gives 2.40 — write the final 0.
Explain why 2.4 would be wrong for '2 decimal places' even though the value looks the same.
Round 9.96 to 1 dp (10.0) and keep the tenths zero.
Check each answer by counting that it shows exactly the required number of decimal places.
activities.insight: A rounded answer must display the required place even when a carry produces a zero there; the trailing zero records the precision, so dropping it changes what the answer claims.

activities.title: Rounding to estimate a calculation
steps: Round each factor of 4.83 × 2.17 to a convenient value (5 × 2) and compute the estimate (10).
Compare your estimate to the exact product once calculated (≈ 10.48) and say whether the estimate is reasonable.
Try estimating another product or sum by rounding each number first, and state which place you rounded to and why.
activities.insight: Rounding has a purpose beyond drill: it gives quick, sensible estimates to check whether an exact calculation is plausible.

checkQuestion: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 3.4567 to 2 decimal places. Round 2.397 to 2 decimal places. Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000.' Watch whether they round or chop, and what they do at the carry.
checkAnswer: 3.46; 2.40 (keeping the final zero); 7,700,000 — deciding by the digit one place beyond the required accuracy.
